1.why: The token digest is stored in the session's recovery record and verification uses a constant-time safeEqual against that session-bound digest, confirming the code belongs to this session/user.

2.why: Recovery records are per-session and compared only against the current session's stored digest, so a code issued in one session cannot verify in another; the statement is false.

3.why: There is no session-invalidation logic anywhere; sessions remain in the map until the 30-minute expiry, so previous sessions genuinely still work after a reset.

4.why: The server is a TLS-only listener that rejects non-HTTPS requests and sets HSTS, but the TLS version is not explicitly pinned to the latest version in the configuration.

5.why: Reset tokens are stored only as SHA-256 digests and passwords are hashed with bcrypt (cost 12); these are appropriate one-way protections, though technically hashing rather than encryption.

6.why: No email is actually sent; the contact value is never transmitted or logged, but the simulated delivery channel exposes the token in plaintext in the browser console and visible logs panel.

7.why: All request bodies are type-validated, tokens are hashed before comparison, passwords are policy-checked and hashed, and the client inserts all data via textContent with server-side escapeHtml for dynamic values.

8.why: Navigation is hash-based routing entirely within the single-page app, no external redirect targets exist, and CSP enforces form-action 'self' and base-uri 'none'.

9.why: No email templates exist, and all dynamic page content is inserted via textContent or escaped HTML under a strict nonce-based CSP, so no user input can appear as script or HTML.

10.why: Error pages are generic with no stack traces, but the reset token and MFA code are deliberately written to console.log and the visible #logs panel, so tokens are shown in logs.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and reset tokens stored as digests, but the MFA secret code is hardcoded in the source as "482913", contradicting the statement.

12.why: No default accounts or credentials exist and a strong password policy is enforced server-side, though the fixed MFA code functions as a shared, predictable code.

13.why: Both per-session throttling and a bounded trusted-IP rate limiter cap attempts (3 for token issuance, 5 for token verification, password submission, and MFA) with 429 responses.

14.why: Every recovery request returns the identical generic message and the contact value is never stored, logged, or checked against any account list, so account existence is not revealed.

15.why: The reset token is a 256-bit CSPRNG value bound to the session, but it is issued without verifying any real user identity and the accompanying MFA code is deterministic ("482913").
